latest_description: Light pollution is an emerging public health hazard that has been linked to elevated risk of many diseases including sleep disorders cancer cardiometabolic diseases dementia and mental disorders. Moreover Light pollution is also an important environmental justice issue. It has been shown that marginalized communities have a disproportionately high burden of Artificial Light At Night (ALAN) and are more susceptible to develope adverse health effects related to alan. Among american cities chicago not only has one of the highest levels of Light pollution but also displays profound injustice in Light pollution. The little village neighborhood in chicago a predominantly mexican immigrant community exemplifies the dual burden of high levels of Light pollution and social vulnerability. Thanks to years of collaborative work with our community partners there is now growing awareness about Light pollution and its detrimental effects among the little village residents. In addition the community members expressed pressing needs in learning more about Light pollution in their neighborhood and taking actions to promote appropriate lighting and mitigate adverse health effects. In particular there are critical needs for 1) an interface that provide high quality data and visualization and analysis tools to characterize the burden of alan 2) a platform that crosslinks alan measures with demographic and socioeconomic indicators and health statistics to demonstrate the scale of Light pollution injustice and highlight its public health implications and 3) an expanded education program that teach students about Light pollution and its consequences and cultivate next-generation activists to take data-informed actions.

Each year the 10-12 student observer cohort will be composed of STEM and stem-interested freshmen sophomores and incoming transfer students from introductory courses. The program will focus on those students not typically served by outreach and engagement programs. Kutztown university has an established 'learning community' approach where a group of students is paired with faculty mentors and meet once a week as a part of their schedule. h2o+h2s will use this program so students are supported with a 1-credit course (1 hour per week) preserving dedicated time for the student observer to fulfill the program without disruption to their academic classes or overburdening schedules. The course will integrate the here to explore program activities with a student-created scientific narrative project based on sharing the mission science. The students observers will develop a short audio/video storytelling project about the NASA mission. Research shows that integrating storytelling or narrative techniques provides powerful access for students of diverse backgrounds to connect with science. Two students from previous cohorts will serve as peer mentors. Scaffolding experiences will include the nasa-led h2o activities fieldtrips professional meeting attendance and mentorship through-out the year. The h2o + h2s program focuses on creating products that articulate workforce skills on student resumes. This directly supports enhanced student success when applying for future internships graduate school and industry jobs.
